title: Instructions and Procedural Content as a Design Object
summary: This capability describes how Creative Navy designs instructions and procedural content as operational artefacts rather than as static documents. The page is grounded in the Assemblio engagement and keeps that evidence within its limits: Creative Navy ran no user research, tested nothing and did not observe a shop floor in that engagement.
keyFacts: Instructions and procedural content as a design object is the capability of designing the artefact that carries procedural know-how: the step-by-step training guide, the experienced worker's lookup surface, the advance review document, and the versioned record that must remain traceable as products change.
Creative Navy treats a work instruction as more than a document: in the Assemblio engagement it had to support training, spot-checking and advance review.
Assemblio is the sole case evidence for this page; no other engagement in the current evidence set designed an instruction artefact.
Creative Navy ran no user research, controlled no research, tested nothing and did not observe a shop floor in the Assemblio engagement.

Assemblio's authoring method derives an assembly sequence by taking a finished 3D model apart and playing the disassembly backwards; this method belongs to Assemblio and has published research provenance.
The Assemblio Composer uses STEP files, folders, projects, products and versions, with product states of Draft, In Review and Approved.
Assemblio reported that cable routing is usually not modelled in CAD and may be documented by a photograph from the experienced worker who routes the first unit.
Each step in Assemblio carries two separate time values: MTM time and animation duration.
Creative Navy designed a flattened parts list for the Assemblio Smart Viewer, refined into tabs for current-step parts and the full hierarchy.

Assemblio's version-and-variant relationships form a graph that can contain loops, and part-level matches require planner approval because Assemblio described the approval record as a liability requirement.

The product is in production, and Creative Navy compared the shipped interface against the delivered designs: the Composer, the Smart Viewer, the platform around them and sync profiles ship as the design that was delivered.

bodySections.heading: Instructions and procedural content as an operational artefact
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Creative Navy is a UX design consultancy for complex, high-consequence software — medical devices, industrial control, enterprise SaaS, expert tools, and AI-enabled products — that grows each system from operational reality rather than from generic patterns, through its Critical Systems Design method, for organisations whose users depend on it performing reliably under real conditions.

Instructions and procedural content become a design problem when an artefact must carry know-how from one population to another. In assembly work, somebody knows how to build the product and somebody else has to build it. The work instruction is the artefact that crosses that gap.

Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats that artefact as a designed product rather than as a document produced after the real work is done. In the Assemblio engagement, the first design distinction was that the instruction was not one thing. It had to support a trainee following steps closely, an experienced worker checking what is different about a variant, and an experienced worker reading the plan in advance before assembling without constant reference.

bodySections.heading: A work instruction can have three reading modes
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A work instruction can serve three different reading modes even when it appears as one artefact. Assemblio described three use cases for the Assemblio Smart Viewer: training, spot-checking and advance review.

In the training use case, a new worker follows the plan step by step and consults the instruction closely. In the spot-check use case, an experienced worker already knows much of the sequence and looks up what is different about this product, part, variant or special case. In the advance review use case, an experienced worker reads the whole plan before starting and then assembles without consulting the instruction continuously.

Creative Navy's design work treated those three modes as structurally different. A step-by-step reader needs clear progression, repeatable playback and controls that stay predictable. A spot-check reader needs fast movement through the plan and a surface that shows the current-step information without forcing the worker through the engineering model. An advance reader needs to understand the complete sequence before work begins.

This distinction separates the instruction artefact from adjacent training-burden problems. Training burden describes the cost of getting people ready to work. This capability is about the object that does part of the teaching, lookup and operational handoff.

bodySections.heading: Procedural content combines CAD data with knowledge that CAD does not contain
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Assemblio's planning workflow begins with source data, but the source data does not contain all procedural knowledge. The Assemblio Composer uses STEP files, where part names come from the design engineer rather than from the language a shop-floor worker would necessarily recognise.

Assemblio's authoring method is inverted. Rather than building the assembly sequence forwards, the planner takes the finished 3D model apart and the software plays that disassembly backwards as the assembly sequence. Assemblio described the reason as avoiding a forward-planning failure where a part cannot be fitted half way through the sequence, forcing the plan to be redone. This method belongs to Assemblio, not to Creative Navy.

The content hierarchy in Assemblio is folders, projects, products and versions. A project is a product family. A folder groups projects, typically by customer. Products evolve continuously, so one product may carry several versions and related products may carry variants of the same plan.

Not all assembly-relevant information exists in the CAD file. Assemblio reported that cable routing is usually not modelled. Assemblio described an established practice in which one experienced worker routes the cables on the first unit, photographs the result and uploads the photograph into the assembly plan for everyone else. Tools can be documented in the same way, with a photograph of the tool to be used for a step.

That makes the instruction a contributed procedural artefact. Engineering data supplies the model and sequence, while worker knowledge can supply missing procedural detail. The design object is therefore not only the exported document; it is the system of relationships between model data, planner decisions, worker feedback, photographs, step records and later retrieval.

bodySections.heading: A procedural step carries sequence, time and workstation structure
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A step in an assembly instruction is not only an item in a list. In Assemblio, each step carries procedural content, visual movement, parts, time values and potential workstation grouping.

Assemblio described two separate time values per step. MTM time records the manual assembly time and sums across the plan so a production engineer can schedule a line. Animation duration controls how long the on-screen movement takes. They are separate because a real assembly step may take hours while the animation must remain watchable in seconds. Assemblio also described cases where users copy the MTM value into the animation duration to see what the step would look like at real speed.

Step groups exist so that a plan can be divided by workstation. Each group can be exported separately for the station that performs it. Assemblio described three outputs for an instruction plan: a PDF, a video and the Smart Viewer itself. The Smart Viewer is not exported in the same sense as the PDF or video; it is accessed as the read surface.

The step is therefore both a procedural unit and a production-planning unit. Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method treats that dual role as part of the interface structure: the worker needs a readable step, while the planner and production engineer need traceability, timing and grouping to remain attached to that step.

bodySections.heading: Shop-floor reading conditions make attention the binding constraint
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Assemblio described the Smart Viewer's user as the shop-floor assembly worker. Assemblio described the environment as bright, dirty and loud, with workers standing, wearing gloves and working at desks filled with tools, parts and paper documents.

Assemblio also reported that input devices are not guaranteed. Workers may have no mouse and no place to put one. Some have a keyboard. Some customers use foot pedals to step forward and back because the worker is standing with both hands occupied. Assemblio described the usual hardware as a tablet on a holder or a monitor beside the workstation with a small PC behind the desk, not a laptop.

In this context, the attention budget is the binding constraint. Assemblio's position was that workers focus on what their hands are doing rather than on the screen, and that controls must be as simple as the task allows. Assemblio also reported that roughly 90% of the time the plan is consulted once and then left playing.

Creative Navy's design response separated the Smart Viewer from the Assemblio Composer as its own interface. Assemblio had already diagnosed that the planning tool and the shop-floor reading surface served different populations. Creative Navy then designed the worker-facing structures inside that separate viewer, including touch and tablet layouts, player controls, a light theme as the shop-floor default, and a shortcut drawer that can be consulted without leaving the step.

bodySections.heading: The engineer's hierarchy is not the worker's parts list
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A CAD hierarchy is useful to engineering, but it is not automatically the right information structure for assembly work. Assemblio reported that the earlier Smart Viewer displayed the complete CAD hierarchy at all times. Assemblio also reported a worked example in which a step contained two visually similar types of screw and the names in the list did not tell the worker which screw was which.

Creative Navy designed a flattened parts list for the Smart Viewer. The list removed hierarchy from the default worker view and carried part quantities. The design was later refined into two tabs: parts needed for the current step, and the full hierarchy. The worker's default is therefore the step-level list, while the complete tree remains reachable for cases that need it.

This is an information-architecture decision. The same parts exist in both structures, but the primary grouping changes from the engineer's product model to the worker's current task. The design does not remove the engineering hierarchy; it changes which structure is primary at the moment of assembly.

The distinction matters because work instructions are often generated from engineering data. The instruction artefact must preserve traceability to the model while presenting the worker with the smallest useful set of parts for the action being performed.

bodySections.heading: Worker feedback turns the instruction into a two-way artefact
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
A work instruction can carry feedback from the floor back to the planner when the feedback is bound to a specific step. Assemblio and its customers had requested a worker comment function before Creative Navy's design work, and Assemblio described the feature as a way for workers to report back to the planner.

Creative Navy designed how the worker-to-planner feedback lives in the Smart Viewer interface. A comment can be raised directly from the 3D canvas as a floating input and attached to a specific assembly step. A Feedback tab in the side panel collects the feedback items.

The step-level binding is important. A general comment channel loses procedural context quickly. A comment attached to the step preserves the relationship between the worker's observation, the part of the sequence being performed and the planner who may need to revise the instruction.

The same design logic applies to confirmable steps, change notifications and old-instruction retrieval, which Assemblio's customer feedback requested. These functions make the instruction an operational record, not only a reading aid.

bodySections.heading: Versions, variants and synchronisation form an information-architecture graph
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Version and variant management is part of instruction design when products change continuously. Assemblio described product relationships as a graph that can contain chains, splits and loops. Synchronisation is scoped within a single project, and a loop can exist where product A is synchronised with product B and product B back with product A.

Assemblio also described a second, harder dimension: part-level matching. Within a synchronisation, every part of the source must be matched to a part of the target. Some parts are identical. Other parts are similar, established by fuzzy comparison where geometry, name or position may differ. The system judges whether the part serves the same function and whether the old plan's step can be transferred to it.

Assemblio's worked example was a vendor no longer supplying a screw. The 3D model changes to a different screw with the same purpose, slightly different geometry and similar position. The planner does not want to redo every animation; the planner wants the existing step transferred onto the new part.

Assemblio stated that the planner must approve each match because the approval is a liability record. The company needs to demonstrate that a person checked the substitution before it went into production. The match list is therefore not only a convenience feature; it is a record of who approved what.

Creative Navy's design work on this area raised questions that surfaced gaps and edge cases, including how an unsynchronised fork should be indicated, whether unsynchronising many relationships needed its own screen, and whether synchronising to an older version should be possible. Assemblio confirmed the old-version use case for long product lifecycles and adopted a resolution in which the latest version is the default while an older version can be selected.

This is why procedural content belongs with information architecture for expert systems. The design problem is not only how to render one instruction. It is how to keep related instructions, products, versions, parts and approvals understandable as a graph over time.

bodySections.heading: Digital instructions create durable retrievability and traceability requirements
bodySections.bodyMarkdown:
Work instructions and digital instructions sit in the broader category of information for use. IEC/IEEE 82079-1 is the standard named in the available research for preparation of information for use. Regulation (EU) 2023/1230, the Machinery Regulation, is relevant to the category because it replaces Machinery Directive 2006/42/EC from 20 January 2027 with no sell-off period for newly built machines and permits digital instructions on condition that they remain accessible for at least ten years.

These references describe the category that Assemblio's output can enter. The design relevance is narrower and more concrete: Assemblio's own shop-floor customers asked for versioning so that an old instruction can be loaded and checked.

The Machinery Regulation's digital-instruction accessibility condition and the customer request land on the same design concern. Old instructions must remain loadable, identifiable and checkable. The supported design claim is that retrievability, versioning and traceability are requirements for the instruction artefact, and that external information-for-use rules make those requirements durable in the domain.

bodySections.heading: What this produces
bodySections.bodyMarkdown: Within Creative Navy's Critical Systems Design method, this capability produces concrete interface design deliverables — interaction design, information architecture, wireframes, screen designs, interactive prototypes, and design-system components — and not advisory documents alone. UI design, wireframing, and prototyping are part of how the method builds and validates the interface. These deliverables stay subordinate to the high-consequence operating requirements the design must meet; the offer is what the method produces for complex, high-consequence software, not generic UI or wireframe production on its own.

strongClaims: Assemblio's authoring method derives an assembly sequence by taking a finished model apart and playing the disassembly backwards; Creative Navy did not design that method.
Creative Navy designed the flattened parts list for the Assemblio Smart Viewer, with current-step parts as the worker default and the full hierarchy still reachable.
Assemblio's version-and-variant relationships form a graph that can contain loops, and part-level matches require planner approval because Assemblio described the approval as a liability record.
Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 permits digital instructions on condition that they remain accessible for at least ten years, but the Assemblio engagement was not compliance work.

The Assemblio product is in production and ships as the design Creative Navy delivered for the Composer, Smart Viewer, surrounding platform and sync profiles. This is design-fidelity evidence, not performance evidence.
weakerClaims: Creative Navy treats instructions and procedural content as a designed artefact with three reading modes: training, spot-checking and advance review. This is grounded in Assemblio's reported Smart Viewer use cases, without Creative Navy-run research or testing.
Assemblio reported shop-floor conditions, input-device variability and attention constraints; Creative Navy did not observe those conditions directly.
Assemblio reports satisfaction with the work and that the work unlocked further funding, but no figures were shared and Creative Navy has not independently verified the claim.
limitations: Assemblio is the only evidence anchor for this capability page; no other engagement in the provided evidence set designed an instruction artefact.
Creative Navy ran no user research, controlled no research, tested nothing and did not observe a shop floor in the Assemblio engagement.
All shop-floor conditions, worker persona details and customer requests are Assemblio-reported rather than Creative Navy-observed.
Assemblio's criticisms of its earlier Smart Viewer are not Creative Navy audit findings and must not be treated as a UX audit.
The disassembly-played-backwards authoring method belongs to Assemblio and must not be attributed to Creative Navy.
No assembly time, error rate, training time, throughput, adoption, revenue or funding figure is established.
No compliance claim is made under IEC/IEEE 82079-1 or Regulation (EU) 2023/1230.
The page does not treat Assemblio as AI work; this capability concerns instruction artefacts, viewer design, traceability, feedback and version relationships.
